cards.q: Besides web browsers, where does JavaScript run?
cards.a:
On servers and in tools via Node.js, Deno or Bun, and in Electron desktop apps

Node.js (and Deno or Bun) run JavaScript on servers and in tools, and Electron apps are built from it. Nobody compiles it ahead of time: the engine compiles hot code on the fly.
cards.lessonTitle: What JavaScript Is and Running It

cards.q: What does TypeScript add to JavaScript?
cards.a:
Types that a checker verifies before the program runs

TypeScript adds static types checked before running. It compiles to plain JavaScript by removing the types, so it runs wherever JavaScript runs.
cards.lessonTitle: What JavaScript Is and Running It

cards.q: What does `console.log("1 + 1 =", 1 + 1)` print?
cards.a:
1 + 1 = 2

The text is printed as it is (without quotes), then a space, then the value of the expression.
cards.lessonTitle: What JavaScript Is and Running It

cards.q: When should you use `let` instead of `const`?
cards.a:
Only when the variable itself must be reassigned later

Use `const` by default and `let` only for a name that must point at a new value. A `const` array or object can still have its contents changed.

cards.q: What does `typeof null` give?
cards.a:
"object"

It gives "object", a historical quirk that cannot be fixed. To check for null, compare with `=== null`.

cards.q: After `const a = [1]; const b = a; b.push(2);`, what is `a`?
cards.a:
[1, 2]

b names the same array; const only stops a from being reassigned, not the array from changing.

cards.q: Why should you prefer `===` to `==`?
cards.a:
`===` compares without converting types, so its result is predictable

`===` needs equal value and equal type, so `1 === "1"` is false. `==` converts its operands with complicated rules, and neither compares the contents of arrays.

cards.q: What is the difference between `a || b` and `a ?? b`?
cards.a:
`||` replaces any falsy `a` (even `0`, `""`); `??` only `null`/`undefined`

`||` gives b for every falsy a, so `0 || 50` is 50. `??` gives b only for null and undefined, so `0 ?? 50` stays 0.

100

"10" + 5 is the string "105"; subtracting converts it to the number 105, giving 100.

cards.q: How do you put the value of `total` into a string?
cards.a:
With a template literal: `` `Total: ${total}` ``

Only backtick strings (template literals) insert `${...}` expressions; in ordinary quotes `${total}` is just text, and without the `$` nothing is inserted.

cards.q: Why is `"😀".length` 2?
cards.a:
The emoji is stored as two UTF-16 code units (a surrogate pair)

JavaScript strings are UTF-16 and `length` counts code units; characters outside the basic range need a pair. `[...text].length` counts real characters.

cards.q: What does `"a-b-c".replace("-", "+")` give?
cards.a:
"a+b-c"

replace with a string argument changes only the first occurrence; replaceAll changes them all.

cards.q: What is the difference between `for...of` and `for...in`?
cards.a:
`for...of` gives the values of an array (any iterable); `for...in` gives object keys

Use `for...of` for arrays and strings; `for...in` is for object keys (on an array it gives the indexes as strings).

cards.q: What happens when a `switch` case has no `break` or `return`?
cards.a:
Execution falls through into the next case

Without break or return, execution carries on into the following case's code. That is handy for grouping cases and a bug when forgotten.

cards.q: How many times does the body of `do { } while (false);` run?
cards.a:
1

A do...while loop checks its condition after the body, so the body always runs at least once.

cards.q: What does an arrow function with braces return if its body has no `return` statement?
cards.a:
`undefined`

With braces the body needs an explicit `return`; without one the function returns `undefined`. Only the one-expression form without braces returns its value automatically.

cards.q: What is the difference between a rest parameter and spread?
cards.a:
Rest collects arguments into an array in a definition; spread expands an array in a call

`function total(...numbers)` gathers the arguments into an array; `total(...prices)` spreads an array out into separate arguments.

cards.q: What does `(() => { value: 1 })()` return?
cards.a:
undefined

The braces are a function body with a label "value", not an object; wrap an object in parentheses to return it.

cards.q: What does `[10, 9, 1].sort()` give?
cards.a:
[1, 10, 9], because without a compare function items are compared as strings

As strings, "10" comes before "9" (the first character "1" is smaller than "9"). Pass `(a, b) => a - b` to sort numbers.

cards.q: Which of `map`, `splice`, `slice` and `sort` change the array they are called on?
cards.a:
`splice` and `sort`

splice and sort change the array in place; map and slice return new arrays. Use `toSorted()` or `[...arr].sort()` for a sorted copy.

cards.q: What is `[1, 2, 3, 4].filter(n => n % 2).map(n => n * 10)`?
cards.a:
[10, 30]

n % 2 is truthy for odd numbers, so 1 and 3 remain, then each is multiplied by 10.

cards.q: When must you use brackets instead of a dot to read a property?
cards.a:
When the name is in a variable or is not an identifier, like "page count"

`book[field]` uses the value of `field` as the name, and `book["page count"]` reaches a name with a space; for fixed, simple names a dot works.

cards.q: Is `{ ...obj }` a deep copy?
cards.a:
No, a shallow copy: nested objects are still shared

Spread makes a new object with the same top-level properties, so nested objects are shared between the copy and the original; `structuredClone(obj)` makes a deep copy.

cards.q: What is `x` after `const { a: x = 5 } = { a: null };`?
cards.a:
null

Defaults apply only when the value is undefined; null is a real value.

cards.q: What is a closure?
cards.a:
A function together with the variables of the scope it was created in

A closure keeps using the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished, which is how `makeCounter` keeps a private count.

cards.q: Why does `let` fix the closure-in-a-loop problem that `var` has?
cards.a:
`let` creates a new binding for each iteration, so each callback keeps its own value

With `var` there is one variable for the whole loop, so every callback sees its final value; `let` gives each round its own `i`.

cards.q: After `let n = 1; const show = () => n; n = 2;`, what does `show()` return?
cards.a:
2

A closure remembers the variable, not its value at the time it was created.

cards.q: When is a Map a better choice than a plain object?
cards.a:
When the keys are data that change at run time or are not strings

Map keys can be any value, it keeps insertion order and has `size`. A record with fixed fields is a plain object, and a Map does not survive JSON.stringify.

cards.q: What does `JSON.stringify` do with a Map?
cards.a:
It writes `{}`, so the entries are lost

Maps (and Sets) become `{}`. Convert first with `Object.fromEntries(map)` (or `[...set]` for a Set).

cards.q: What is `new Set("hello").size`?
cards.a:
4

A string is iterable, giving h, e, l, l, o; the set keeps the 4 distinct letters.

cards.q: What does a `#` in front of a field name, as in `#balance`, mean?
cards.a:
The field is private: only code inside the class body can use it

`#` fields can be read and written only by code inside the class; `acc.#balance` outside it is a SyntaxError. Static members are marked with `static`.

cards.q: Why must a subclass constructor call `super()` before it uses `this`?
cards.a:
The parent's constructor sets up the object; `this` does not exist until it has run

In a class with `extends`, the object is created by the parent's constructor, so using `this` before `super(...)` throws a ReferenceError.

cards.q: A class `Thing` has `static create() {}`. How is it called?
cards.a:
Thing.create()

Static members belong to the class itself, not to its instances.

cards.q: Where does a class's method live?
cards.a:
Once on `ClassName.prototype`; instances find it through the prototype chain

Methods are stored once on the prototype and every instance links to it, which is why `Object.keys(p)` shows only the instance's own fields.

cards.q: Why does `setTimeout(obj.method, 100)` often break?
cards.a:
The method is called later on its own, so `this` is not obj

Passing `obj.method` hands over the function alone; called later without `obj.` in front, `this` is undefined. Pass `() => obj.method()` or `obj.method.bind(obj)`.

cards.q: Inside an arrow function defined in a class method, what is `this`?
cards.a:
the same this as in the method

Arrow functions have no this of their own; they use the surrounding one.

cards.q: Why `throw new Error("...")` instead of `throw "..."`?
cards.a:
Error objects carry a name, a message and a stack, and work with instanceof

Any value can be thrown and caught, but an Error tells you what went wrong and where (its stack), and callers can check its type with `instanceof`.

cards.q: What should a `catch` block do with an error it does not know how to handle?
cards.a:
Rethrow it, so it is not silently hidden

Catch only what you can handle: check the type, deal with your own errors and `throw err` for the rest, or bugs such as a ReferenceError from a typo are hidden.

cards.q: What does `f()` return, where `function f() { try { return "try"; } finally { console.log("cleanup"); } }`?
cards.a:
"try", after printing cleanup

finally runs before the return completes, but does not change the value unless it returns itself.

cards.q: What makes an object usable in `for...of`?
cards.a:
A `[Symbol.iterator]()` method returning an iterator whose `next()` gives `{ value, done }`

That is the iteration protocol used by `for...of`, spread and destructuring. Plain objects and class instances do not have it unless you add it; use `Object.entries` for objects.

cards.q: Why can a generator describe an infinite sequence such as `naturals()`?
cards.a:
It is lazy: it computes the next value only when asked, so a consumer can stop

Each `yield` pauses the generator until the next value is requested. A consumer such as `take` that stops early means the loop never runs forever.

cards.q: What is `[...take(naturals(), 3)]` after `[...take(naturals(), 3)]` was already spread once?
cards.a:
[1, 2, 3]

Each call to take(naturals(), 3) creates new generators, so it starts again from 1.

cards.q: What is the difference between `import { x } from "./m.js"` and `import x from "./m.js"`?
cards.a:
`{ x }` takes the named export `x`; `x` alone takes the default export under any name

With braces you name a named export exactly (or rename it with `as`); without braces you get the module's one default export and choose the name yourself.

cards.q: If two files import the same module, does the module run twice?
cards.a:
No: it runs once, and both files share the same instance and its state

Each module runs the first time it is imported; later imports get the same instance, so a module-level `let` is shared by every importer.

cards.q: A module has `export let count = 0; export function inc() { count++; }`. Another file runs `inc()` then reads `count`. What does it see?
cards.a:
1

Imports are live bindings to the exporting module's variables.

cards.q: Why does `setTimeout(f, 0)` not run `f` immediately?
cards.a:
It puts `f` in the task queue, which runs only after the current code and the microtasks

The event loop takes the next task only when the stack is empty and all waiting microtasks have run, so `f` always runs after the current code.

cards.q: What happens to a web page while a long synchronous loop runs?
cards.a:
It freezes: no events, timers or redraws can run until the loop ends

JavaScript runs one thing at a time on one thread, so while your code runs nothing else can. Long work belongs in small pieces or in a Web Worker you create.

cards.q: In what order are these printed: `setTimeout(() => log("A"))`, `Promise.resolve().then(() => log("B"))`, `log("C")`?
cards.a:
C B A

Synchronous code first, then microtasks (promises), then tasks (timers).

cards.q: What does `promise.then(f)` return?
cards.a:
A new promise for what `f` returns, waiting for it if that is a promise

`then` returns a new promise straight away; it fulfils with f's return value, or follows it if f returns a promise, which is what keeps chains flat.

cards.q: What is the difference between `Promise.all` and `Promise.allSettled`?
cards.a:
`all` rejects as soon as one rejects; `allSettled` waits for all and reports each outcome

`allSettled` never rejects: it fulfils with `{ status, value }` or `{ status, reason }` for each promise. Both start everything at once; `Promise.any` is the one with AggregateError.

cards.q: `Promise.resolve(1).then(x => { throw new Error("no"); }).then(x => 2).catch(e => 3)` fulfils with:
cards.a:
3

The throw rejects the chain, the second then is skipped, and catch returns 3.

cards.q: What does an `async` function return if its body says `return 5`?
cards.a:
A promise that fulfils with 5

An async function always returns a promise; its `return` value becomes the fulfilled value, and a `throw` rejects it.

cards.q: Why is `ids.forEach(async id => { ... })` a bug when you need to wait for the work?
cards.a:
forEach ignores the promises the callback returns, so nothing waits and errors go unhandled

forEach starts every callback and returns at once. Use `for...of` with `await` for one at a time, or `await Promise.all(ids.map(...))` for all at once.

cards.q: `const [a, b] = await Promise.all([slowA(), slowB()])`, where each takes 1 second, takes about:
cards.a:
1 second

Both operations are started before the await, so they run at the same time.

cards.q: Does `fetch` reject when the server answers 404?
cards.a:
No: it fulfils with `response.ok` false, so you check `ok` or `status`

fetch rejects only when the request cannot be made at all (no network, a bad URL, a blocked request). A 404 or 500 is still a response.

cards.q: How do you send a JavaScript object as a JSON body with `fetch`?
cards.a:
Use `method: "POST"`, a JSON `Content-Type` header and `body: JSON.stringify(object)`

The body must be text, so `JSON.stringify` turns the object into JSON; the header tells the server what the text is. `JSON.parse` goes the other way, from text to a value.

cards.q: What is `String(new URLSearchParams({ a: "x y", b: 1 }))`?
cards.a:
a=x+y&b=1

URLSearchParams escapes values, writing spaces as +, and has no leading ?.

cards.q: What is the difference between debounce and throttle?
cards.a:
Debounce runs once after the calls stop for a while; throttle runs at most once per period

A debounced search waits until typing pauses, then runs once; a throttled drag handler keeps running, but never more than once per period.

cards.q: In `mapLimit`, why is `next++` safe without locks, even with several workers?
cards.a:
JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time; a worker can only pause at an `await`

All workers share the one `next` through a closure, but code runs on one thread and a worker is only interrupted at an `await`, never in the middle of `const i = next++`.

cards.q: A debounced function with 100 ms is called at 0, 50 and 120 ms. When does it run?
cards.a:
At 220 ms only

Each call restarts the wait; the last call at 120 ms runs 100 ms later because no call follows it.

cards.q: Does TypeScript check types while the program runs?
cards.a:
No: they are checked before running, then removed

Types exist only while you write and check the code; tsc strips them and the running code is plain JavaScript. Strict mode makes the compile-time checks stricter, it adds nothing at run time.

cards.q: Why prefer `unknown` over `any` for data from `JSON.parse`?
cards.a:
`unknown` must be checked before use; `any` switches checking off

Both accept every value, and neither does anything at run time; the difference is that `unknown` must be narrowed before use, so mistakes are caught.

cards.q: What type does TypeScript infer for `const names = []` under strict mode, before anything is pushed?
cards.a:
An evolving `any[]` that takes the types you push

An empty array literal gets an evolving type; writing `const names: string[] = []` states the intent up front.

cards.q: An object has more properties than an interface asks for. Can it be passed where the interface is expected?
cards.a:
Yes, from a variable; only a fresh object literal is rejected

Types are compared by shape, so extra properties do not matter. Only an object literal written in place is checked for unknown properties, because that is usually a typo; nothing is removed at run time.

cards.q: What is the difference between `extends` on an interface and `&` on types?
cards.a:
Both combine members: `extends` builds a new interface, `&` an intersection type

Both give a type with all the members of the parts. `&` is an intersection (a union is written `|`), and neither exists at run time.

cards.q: Which declares an object whose keys are any strings and values are booleans?
cards.a:
type Flags = Record<string, boolean>

Record<K, V> (or an index signature [key: string]: boolean) describes a dictionary. `{ string: boolean }` is an object with one property named "string".

cards.q: What makes a union discriminated?
cards.a:
Each variant has a shared tag property with its own literal type

Checking the shared tag property narrows the value to one variant. Interface names do not exist at run time, so they cannot be checked.

cards.q: What does assigning the value to a variable of type `never` in the `default` case achieve?
cards.a:
Compiling fails if any variant is left unhandled

If a variant has no case, the value in `default` is still that variant, not `never`, so the assignment is a compile error that points at the switch to update.

cards.q: Given `x: string | number[]`, which check narrows `x` to `string`?
cards.a:
if (typeof x === "string")

Both types have length; typeof distinguishes the primitive string. instanceof String checks for String objects, not string values.

cards.q: In `function f<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K)`, what does `K extends keyof T` mean?
cards.a:
K must be one of the property names of T

`keyof T` is the union of T's property names, and `extends` limits K to that union, so a wrong name is a compile error.

cards.q: Why is `first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined` better than `first(items: any[]): any`?
cards.a:
The result keeps the element type, so it is still checked

The type parameter connects input and output: `first([3, 1])` gives `number | undefined`, while `any` switches checking off for the result. Both accept every array.

cards.q: For `pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(items: T[], key: K): T[K][]` called with users and "age", the result type is:
cards.a:
number[]

T[K] is the type of the age property, number, so the result is number[].

cards.q: What is the difference between `private` and `#` in a TypeScript class?
cards.a:
`private` is only checked by the compiler; `#` is private at run time too

TypeScript removes `private` when it compiles, so plain JavaScript can still read the field; `#` is JavaScript's own private field syntax.

cards.q: What does `Partial<Omit<Todo, "id">>` describe?
cards.a:
Any subset of Todo's fields except id, all optional

Omit removes id, then Partial makes every remaining property optional, which is what an update needs.

cards.q: What is `typeof LEVELS[number]` when `const LEVELS = ["a", "b"] as const`?
cards.a:
"a" | "b"

Indexing the readonly tuple type with number gives the union of its element types. Without as const it would just be string.

cards.q: What does `document.querySelector` return when nothing matches?
cards.a:
`null`

It returns the first match or null, so a misspelled selector shows up later as "Cannot read properties of null". querySelectorAll is the one that gives an empty NodeList.

cards.q: Why is `el.innerHTML = userText` dangerous?
cards.a:
The text is parsed as HTML, so it can inject elements and scripts

Parsing user text as HTML allows cross-site scripting (XSS); textContent shows the text exactly as typed.

cards.q: Which escape must come first when escaping text for HTML?
cards.a:
& to &

Replacing & later would turn the & of the other entities, such as <, into &lt;.

cards.q: Why does one click listener on a `<ul>` also work for list items added later?
cards.a:
Clicks bubble from the item up to the ul, where the listener sees them

That is event delegation: the listener sits on the parent, and `event.target.closest(...)` finds which item was clicked.

cards.q: What type are the values from `new FormData(form)`?
cards.a:
Strings (or File objects for file inputs)

Even `<input type="number">` gives "36", not 36, so convert values yourself.

cards.q: A form's submit handler does not call event.preventDefault(). What happens?
cards.a:
The browser submits the form and loads a new page

Submitting a form is the default action; without preventDefault the page navigates away, interrupting your code's work.

cards.q: What does `localStorage.getItem` return for a key that was never set?
cards.a:
`null`

getItem gives null for a missing key, which is why the lesson writes `?? "[]"` before JSON.parse.

cards.q: Why wrap `JSON.parse` of stored data in try/catch?
cards.a:
Stored data may be corrupt or unavailable; reading must not crash

Data may have been cut off, changed by an extension or written by another version, and storage may be blocked; catching the error lets you fall back to defaults.

cards.q: You store `localStorage.setItem("count", 5)`. What does `localStorage.getItem("count")` return?
cards.a:
"5"

Storage keeps strings only; the number is converted to "5".

cards.q: Which versions does `^2.3.1` allow?
cards.a:
From 2.3.1 up to, but not including, 3.0.0

The caret allows new minor and patch versions but not a new major one; the tilde (`~2.3.1`) is the one that stops below 2.4.0.

cards.q: Why commit package-lock.json?
cards.a:
It pins exact versions, so every install gets the same code

It records the exact version of every package, and `npm ci` installs exactly that; scripts and the name live in package.json.

cards.q: Which belongs in devDependencies?
cards.a:
The test runner

devDependencies are tools needed only while developing and building, like test runners and compilers.

cards.q: Why keep update and render free of DOM and storage calls?
cards.a:
They stay pure, so they can be tested without a browser

All side effects then live in one small place (main.ts), and the pure parts are easy to test and reason about.

cards.q: Why must render escape habit names?
cards.a:
The string becomes innerHTML, so names could inject markup

The HTML string is assigned to innerHTML, so unescaped user text could add elements or scripts (XSS).

cards.q: In this design, what happens when the user clicks a habit's toggle button?
cards.a:
An action goes to update; the new state is saved and rendered

All changes go through actions and update; the DOM is only ever drawn from state.

cards.q: On the text `"a" and "b"`, what is the difference between `".+"` and `".+?"`?
cards.a:
The first runs to the last quote; the second stops at the first

Quantifiers are greedy and take as much as they can; adding ? makes them lazy, so they stop as soon as the rest can match.

cards.q: When do you need `new RegExp(...)` instead of `/.../`?
cards.a:
When the pattern is only known at run time

A literal is fixed when you write the code. Flags, named groups and matchAll all work with literals too.

cards.q: What does "a1b22".match(/\d+/g) return?
cards.a:
[ '1', '22' ]

With g, match returns every match; \d+ takes as many digits as it can each time.

cards.q: Why does `Object.freeze(settings)` not stop `settings.sizes.push(3)`?
cards.a:
Freezing is shallow: the array inside is not frozen

The property `sizes` cannot be replaced, but the array it points to is a separate object that was never frozen.

cards.q: Why use a Symbol as a property key instead of a string?
cards.a:
A symbol is unique, so it cannot clash with any other property

Two symbols are different even with the same description, and symbol keys stay out of Object.keys, for...in and JSON. Any key can be made non-enumerable with defineProperty.

cards.q: An object has a getter `area` and no setter. In a module, what does `shape.area = 5` do?
cards.a:
throws a TypeError

Modules are strict mode, where assigning to a property with only a getter is an error. Outside strict mode it would be silently ignored.

cards.q: Why call `Reflect.set(...)` inside a `set` trap instead of `obj[key] = value`?
cards.a:
It does the default assignment and returns whether it worked

Reflect.set handles setters and the receiver like a normal assignment and returns true or false, which the trap must return. Writing to the target does not run the trap; only writes to the proxy do.

cards.q: Why can a WeakMap not be iterated?
cards.a:
Its entries vanish when the garbage collector removes their keys

Its contents depend on when the garbage collector runs, so they are not something code could rely on.

cards.q: Which suits "remember extra data about objects owned by someone else, without keeping them alive"?
cards.a:
WeakMap

A WeakMap entry goes away when nothing else refers to its key object; a Map would keep the object alive.

cards.q: Why should money be stored in whole cents?
cards.a:
Decimal fractions are not exact as doubles, but whole numbers are

0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, so sums of fractions drift; whole cents add exactly and are formatted at the end.

cards.q: What is `new Date(2026, 0, 31)`?
cards.a:
31 January 2026, in local time

Months count from 0, so 0 is January, and these number arguments are read in local time; Date.UTC(...) gives UTC.

cards.q: What does 10n + 5 do?
cards.a:
throws a TypeError: the two cannot be mixed

BigInt and number cannot be mixed in arithmetic; convert one of them first with BigInt(...) or Number(...).

cards.q: What is `keyof { a: number; b: string }`?
cards.a:
`"a" | "b"`

keyof gives the union of the property names; `T[keyof T]` would give the union of the value types.

cards.q: What does `satisfies` give you that a type annotation does not?
cards.a:
The value is checked but keeps its own, more precise type

With an annotation the variable takes the wide annotated type; with satisfies, `palette.green` is still known to be a string.

cards.q: What is ElementOf<string[]> with type ElementOf<T> = T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? E : never?
cards.a:
string

infer E captures the element type of the array.

cards.q: Why read a huge file as a stream instead of with `readFile`?
cards.a:
A stream handles one piece at a time, so memory use stays flat

readFile loads the whole file into memory; a stream read with for await keeps only the current piece.

cards.q: What does `process.exit(2)` tell the program that started yours?
cards.a:
That it failed: any non-zero exit code means failure

0 means success; any other number means failure, and the number can say which kind.

cards.q: Which is the ES module way to bring in path?
cards.a:
import path from "node:path";

import is ES modules; require is the older CommonJS system.

cards.q: What is the difference between a `Uint8Array` and a `DataView` over the same buffer?
cards.a:
A DataView reads any number type at any offset and byte order

A Uint8Array sees the buffer as single bytes (one element type). Both are views of the same memory, and both can read and write.

cards.q: Why is `"café".length` different from its UTF-8 byte count?
cards.a:
`length` counts UTF-16 units; UTF-8 needs two bytes for `é`

`"café".length` is 4, but its UTF-8 form has 5 bytes: one each for c, a and f, two for é.

cards.q: A Uint8Array element is set to 300. What does it hold?
cards.a:
44, because it wraps around modulo 256

Uint8Array wraps modulo 256 (300 - 256 = 44). Uint8ClampedArray would hold 255.

cards.q: Why does breaking out of the paging loop save requests?
cards.a:
The generator fetches a page only when the loop asks for more

The generator is lazy: after break nothing asks for the next item, so page 3 is never requested.

cards.q: What runs when a `for await` loop ends early with `break`?
cards.a:
The generator's `return()` is called, so its `finally` runs

break, return or an exception tells the generator to finish, which runs any finally inside it so it can close connections.

cards.q: Which declares an async generator?
cards.a:
async function* gen() { yield 1; }

The star after function makes it a generator; async in front lets it await.

cards.q: Who holds the AbortController and who gets the signal?
cards.a:
The code that may cancel keeps the controller; the work gets only the signal

The work can listen for abort but cannot cancel anything; only whoever holds the controller can call abort().

cards.q: Why should a cancellable wait remove its abort listener when it finishes normally?
cards.a:
The signal can outlive the wait, so leftover listeners leak memory

Listeners left on a long-lived signal keep their closures alive and would run later for no reason.

cards.q: What does fetch do when its signal is aborted?
cards.a:
stops the request and rejects with an AbortError

The promise rejects, with an error whose name is "AbortError".

cards.q: Why does `assert.equal({ a: 1 }, { a: 1 })` fail with node:assert/strict?
cards.a:
It compares with ===, and these are two different objects

=== compares objects by identity, so two objects with the same contents are not equal; deepEqual compares contents.

cards.q: How can a test check that a function sent an email without sending one?
cards.a:
Pass the send function in and give the test a spy

The code under test receives send as a parameter; the spy records its arguments, which the test then checks.

cards.q: An async test calls assert.rejects(p) without await. What happens?
cards.a:
the test can finish and pass before the check runs

Without await the test function returns before the promise settles, so a failure is not reported for that test.

cards.q: After `const next = { ...state, items: [...state.items, x] }`, which parts of `next` are shared with `state`?
cards.a:
Every property except `items`

Spread copies one level: `next.items` is a new array, while every other property points at the same values as in `state`.

cards.q: What is the difference between `sort` and `toSorted`?
cards.a:
sort reorders the array in place; toSorted returns a sorted copy

Both compare the same way (as strings unless you pass a compare function); toSorted leaves the original alone.

cards.q: Which copies nested objects, Maps and Dates?
cards.a:
structuredClone(obj)

Spread and Object.assign copy one level, and freeze copies nothing; structuredClone copies all the way down.
